title: Meals of the Day & Traditional Dishes
description: Discuss daily meal times, describe traditional dishes, and express flavours and tastes.
objectives: Identify the four main eating occasions (breakfast, lunch, dinner, snack)
Use taste and texture adjectives (spicy, sweet, savoury, fresh, bitter)
Describe famous South Asian and international dishes in simple present sentences

vocabularyList.definition: A meal eaten in the morning, the first of the day.
vocabularyList.exampleSentence: We have breakfast together at 7:30 AM.

vocabularyList.definition: A meal eaten in the middle of the day, typically one that is lighter than an evening meal.
vocabularyList.exampleSentence: I bring a homemade lunch to the office.

vocabularyList.definition: The main meal of the day, taken in the evening.
vocabularyList.exampleSentence: The whole family gathers for dinner at eight.

vocabularyList.definition: Any of the regular occasions in a day when a reasonably large amount of food is eaten.
vocabularyList.exampleSentence: Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.

vocabularyList.definition: A small amount of food eaten between meals.
vocabularyList.exampleSentence: He eats fresh almonds as an afternoon snack.

vocabularyList.definition: The sweet course eaten at the end of a meal.
vocabularyList.exampleSentence: Kheer is a traditional Pakistani dessert.

vocabularyList.definition: Flavoured with or fragrant with spice; pungent or hot.
vocabularyList.exampleSentence: Lahori street food is wonderfully spicy.

vocabularyList.definition: Having the pleasant taste characteristic of sugar or honey.
Recently made or obtained; not canned, frozen, or stale.
vocabularyList.exampleSentence: We buy fresh vegetables from the local market.

vocabularyList.definition: Feeling or displaying the need for food.
vocabularyList.exampleSentence: I am hungry after a long day at university.

sections.title: Daily Meals & Describing Flavours
sections.content:
In English, we use specific verbs with meals:
- **have breakfast / eat breakfast** (never *'drink breakfast'* or *'take breakfast'* in modern native English).
- **have lunch / have dinner / have a snack**.

### Flavour Adjectives
- **spicy**: hot with chillies and spices (*spicy biryani*)
- **sweet**: containing sugar or honey (*sweet halwa*)
- **savoury**: salty and rich in flavour, not sweet (*savoury samosas*)
- **sour**: sharp acidic taste (*sour lemon juice*)
- **bitter**: harsh, non-sweet taste (*bitter black coffee*)

tables.title: Meal Times & Traditional Dishes
rows: I have a paratha and chai for breakfast.
She eats daal chawal for lunch.
We enjoy savoury samosas with evening tea.
They eat chicken biryani for dinner.

callouts.title: Have vs. Take
callouts.text: In British and American English, native speakers say **have breakfast**, **have lunch**, or **have dinner**. Saying *'I take dinner'* sounds old-fashioned or unnatural.

sections.title: Lesson Summary
summaryPoints: Four meal occasions: breakfast (morning), lunch (midday), snack (light bite), dinner (evening).
Use the collocation 'have breakfast / have lunch / have dinner'.
Taste adjectives: spicy, sweet, savoury, sour, bitter.
Dessert (double s) = sweet course; Desert (single s) = sandy region.
Hungry = needs food; Thirsty = needs drink.
